source_text: Ita ergo ut ad causam referamus exemplum, intellegere potuisti vel definitione non liberi, quid deberes liberum nuncupare. Nam etsi in liberi arbitrii definitione intellegentia caligasset, ut id dici liberum posse arbitrareris, quod inter duo contraria uni doceretur adhaerere, respicere debuisti exponi aliter non posse captivum, id est non liberum, quam ut inter duo contraria uni vindicaretur addictum, et ideo nomen libertati captivitatis negatione tribuendum, ut, quoniam id, quod liberum non erat, alteri de contrariis cogeretur adhaerere, illud adversum ei id est liberum neutro sineretur addici.
pass_a_gloss: Thus therefore that we may refer the example to the cause, you could have understood even by the definition of the not-free what you ought to name free. For even if in the definition of free choice intelligence had darkened, so that you would judge that could be said free which among two contraries would be taught to cling to one, you ought to have looked that a captive, that is not free, cannot be exposed otherwise than that among two contraries it be vindicated addicted to one, and therefore the name to be attributed to liberty by the negation of captivity, so that, since that which was not free was forced to cling to one of the contraries, that adverse to it, that is the free, would be allowed to be addicted to neither.

lemmas.lexica: LS liber=free; also children; context decides

pass_b_english: To apply the example to our case, then: you could have understood what to call free from the definition of unfree. Even if your understanding grew dark when defining free will, so that you thought something could be called free while confined to one of two opposites, you should have noticed that captivity—that is, lack of freedom—can be explained only as being bound to one of two opposites. Freedom must therefore be named by denying captivity. Since what is unfree is forced to cling to one of the opposites, its contrary, what is free, cannot be bound to either.

choices.why: Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.
